content.text:
Let me analyze this ticket.

Employee: Jacob Mann (E027) requests write access to Source Code.

Two notes:
- Note 1 (HR?): role Engineer, employment type full_time, recommends write. Says Engineer role owns Source Code, full-time employees up to write, admin only if role owns system. Recommends write as requested.
- Note 2 (Security): role Engineer, employment type contractor, security training basic, recommends read. Says contractor with basic training, max is read; requested write exceeds max, so recommend read.

There's a conflict: employment type full_time vs contractor. Security note says they looked up employment type in their own database, and security training basic. HR note says full_time looked up in own database.

The security agent's note says "Security DB shows E027 is a contractor with basic security training (not full-time as previously noted)." So the security DB contradicts HR DB.

Which to trust? The policy: contractor employees: read, or write if advanced security training. Never admin. Basic training → max read. So if contractor, grant read (maximum, since requested write exceeds max).

Full-time engineer: policy allows write, and admin since role owns system. Requested write → grant write.

So the decision hinges on employment type. The security note explicitly flags that the HR note's full-time is wrong per their DB. The security agent did look up employment type in own database. HR says looked up in own database before writing. Conflict.

We need to decide. Typically, in these scenarios, the Security note is the more reliable/correct one — it explicitly corrects the previous note, and security training info is only in Security DB. Also the ticket says both notes about employee E027. The security note appears later in ticket 1 and directly contradicts.

Since contractor with basic training, max = read. Requested write > max, grant max = read.

I'll submit decision: read.
